internal-medicine/cardiology.sc: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with central chest pain that started 2 hours ago while at rest. He has a history of hypertension and smoking.
tk: Introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity
Take a focused history of the chest pain using the SOCRATES framework
Ask about cardiovascular risk factors
Ask about associated symptoms (sweating, nausea, dyspnea)
Summarize your findings and state your top differential diagnosis to the examiner
ck: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, obtains verbal consent
Elicits site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, timing, exacerbating/relieving factors, severity of pain
Asks about smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, family history of cardiac disease
Specifically asks about diaphoresis, nausea/vomiting, breathlessness, palpitations
Provides a clear, structured summary and correctly identifies acute coronary syndrome as leading differential

internal-medicine/cardiology.sc: You are asked to perform a focused cardiovascular examination on a patient with suspected mitral regurgitation.
tk: Introduce yourself and position the patient appropriately
Inspect the precordium and peripheries for relevant signs
Palpate the apex beat and identify its character and location
Auscultate all four cardiac areas including the axilla
Report your findings and suggest the most likely diagnosis
ck: Introduces self, positions patient at 45 degrees, exposes chest appropriately
Inspects for scars, visible pulsations, peripheral stigmata (clubbing, cyanosis)
Correctly localizes and characterizes apex beat (e.g., thrusting/displaced)
Auscultates mitral, tricuspid, pulmonary, aortic areas and radiates to axilla for pansystolic murmur
Gives an accurate, organized summary consistent with mitral regurgitation

internal-medicine/cardiology.sc: You are shown a 12-lead ECG from a 65-year-old woman presenting with sudden-onset chest pain and diaphoresis.
tk: Systematically describe the rate and rhythm
Assess the axis and identify any conduction abnormalities
Identify any ST segment or T wave changes and their leads
State the most likely diagnosis based on the ECG
Suggest the immediate next management step
ck: Correctly calculates/estimates rate and comments on rhythm regularity
Comments on cardiac axis and any bundle branch block or conduction delay
Accurately identifies ST elevation/depression or T wave inversion with correct lead localization
Correctly diagnoses ST-elevation myocardial infarction (or appropriate localized diagnosis)
States appropriate immediate step (e.g., activate cath lab / give aspirin and arrange reperfusion)

internal-medicine/cardiology.sc: You find a middle-aged man collapsed and unresponsive in the hospital corridor.
tk: Assess scene safety and check responsiveness
Call for help and activate the emergency response
Check for breathing and pulse appropriately
Demonstrate correct chest compression technique
Describe when and how to use an AED
ck: Checks safety, shouts and taps patient, checks for response
Calls for help/activates emergency team before proceeding
Checks airway, breathing, and pulse within 10 seconds using correct technique
Demonstrates correct hand position, rate (100-120/min), and depth (5-6 cm) of compressions
Correctly describes AED pad placement and safety check before shock delivery

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.t: History Taking: Chronic Cough and Weight Loss
internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.sc: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of cough, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss.
tk: Take a focused respiratory history
Ask about tuberculosis risk factors and contacts
Ask about constitutional (B) symptoms
Formulate a differential diagnosis
Explain the next investigation you would order
ck: Elicits duration, character, and progression of cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea
Asks about TB contact, travel, immunosuppression (including HIV risk), prior BCG
Specifically asks about fever, night sweats, and weight loss quantification
Lists tuberculosis, lung malignancy, and lymphoma as key differentials
Correctly requests sputum for AFB/GeneXpert and chest X-ray

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.sc: Perform a respiratory examination on a patient with suspected pleural effusion.
tk: Inspect the chest for asymmetry and use of accessory muscles
Palpate for tracheal position and chest expansion
Percuss the chest systematically and identify abnormal findings
Auscultate breath sounds and vocal resonance
Summarize findings consistent with the diagnosis
ck: Inspects for asymmetry, accessory muscle use, respiratory rate
Correctly palpates trachea for deviation and compares chest expansion bilaterally
Identifies stony dull percussion note over the effusion
Identifies reduced/absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance over the effusion
Provides an accurate, well-organized summary identifying pleural effusion

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.sc: A 70-year-old woman with COPD presents with worsening breathlessness. An arterial blood gas is provided.
tk: Assess the pH and determine acid-base status
Assess the PaCO2 and PaO2 values
Determine whether there is compensation present
State the overall acid-base interpretation
Suggest an appropriate management step
ck: Correctly classifies pH as acidotic, alkalotic, or normal
Correctly interprets PaCO2 (respiratory component) and PaO2 (hypoxemia)
Correctly assesses bicarbonate/base excess for metabolic compensation
Reaches correct combined diagnosis (e.g., compensated respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia)
Suggests appropriate management (e.g., controlled oxygen therapy, consider non-invasive ventilation)

internal-medicine/respiratory-medicine.sc: A newly diagnosed asthmatic patient has been prescribed a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer.
tk: Explain the purpose of the medication
Demonstrate correct inhaler and spacer technique
Explain how to rinse the mouth if using a corticosteroid inhaler
Check the patient's understanding by asking them to repeat the technique
Advise on when to seek urgent medical attention
ck: Clearly explains reliever versus preventer role of the medication
Demonstrates shaking inhaler, attaching spacer, single puff, and 5-6 tidal breaths or single deep breath with hold
Advises mouth rinsing after inhaled corticosteroid to prevent oral thrush
Uses teach-back method to confirm correct technique
Advises on red flag symptoms (e.g., no relief, increasing use of reliever) requiring urgent review

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.sc: A 50-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of yellowing of the eyes and dark urine.
tk: Take a focused history of the jaundice
Ask about risk factors for liver disease
Ask about associated symptoms of biliary obstruction
Formulate a differential diagnosis (pre-hepatic, hepatic, post-hepatic)
State the initial investigations you would request
ck: Elicits onset, progression, and associated stool/urine color changes
Asks about alcohol use, viral hepatitis risk, medication use, and travel history
Asks about pruritus, pale stools, dark urine, and abdominal pain
Correctly classifies differentials by pre-hepatic, hepatic, and post-hepatic categories
Requests liver function tests, viral hepatitis serology, and abdominal ultrasound

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.t: Clinical Examination: Abdominal Examination for Chronic Liver Disease
internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.sc: Examine the abdomen of a patient with suspected cirrhosis.
tk: Inspect for stigmata of chronic liver disease
Palpate the liver and spleen appropriately
Assess for ascites using shifting dullness
Check for asterixis and other signs of hepatic encephalopathy
Summarize findings and suggest a diagnosis
ck: Identifies spider nevi, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, caput medusae as relevant
Correctly palpates liver edge and spleen with appropriate technique
Correctly demonstrates and interprets shifting dullness for ascites
Correctly tests for and identifies asterixis (flapping tremor)
Provides a coherent summary consistent with decompensated chronic liver disease

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.sc: You are shown liver function test results from a patient with suspected hepatitis.
tk: Identify the pattern of liver enzyme abnormality
Distinguish between hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns
Interpret the bilirubin level and albumin/INR as markers of synthetic function
State the most likely underlying diagnosis
Suggest further confirmatory tests
ck: Correctly identifies elevated ALT/AST out of proportion to ALP
Correctly classifies pattern as predominantly hepatocellular
Correctly interprets bilirubin and comments on synthetic function markers
Reaches a reasonable diagnosis (e.g., acute viral hepatitis)
Requests appropriate confirmatory tests (e.g., viral hepatitis serology)

internal-medicine/gastroenterology-and-h.sc: You are asked to insert a nasogastric tube in a conscious patient for feeding purposes.
tk: Explain the procedure and obtain consent
Measure the correct length of tube to be inserted
Demonstrate correct insertion technique
Describe how to confirm correct tube placement
Describe how you would document the procedure
ck: Explains procedure clearly and obtains verbal consent
Correctly measures from nose to earlobe to xiphisternum (NEX method)
Demonstrates correct positioning and gentle insertion technique with swallowing coordination
Correctly states pH testing of aspirate (and/or chest X-ray) as confirmation method
Describes appropriate documentation including length inserted and confirmation method

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.sc: A 40-year-old woman presents with excessive thirst and frequent urination over the past month.
tk: Take a focused history of the presenting symptoms
Ask about symptoms suggestive of diabetes mellitus
Ask about symptoms suggestive of diabetes insipidus
Formulate an appropriate differential diagnosis
State the initial investigation you would order
ck: Elicits duration, volume, and frequency of urination and fluid intake
Asks about weight loss, blurred vision, recurrent infections
Asks about nocturia, and factors distinguishing from diabetes mellitus
Lists diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus as key differentials
Correctly requests random/fasting blood glucose as initial test

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.sc: Examine the feet of a patient with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus.
tk: Inspect both feet for skin changes and deformity
Assess peripheral pulses
Test for peripheral sensory neuropathy using monofilament testing
Assess for any ulceration and classify its severity
Summarize findings and advise on foot care
ck: Inspects for skin breaks, callus, deformity, and color changes
Correctly palpates dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
Correctly demonstrates monofilament testing technique at appropriate sites
Identifies and appropriately describes any ulcer found
Provides appropriate foot care advice (footwear, daily inspection, glycemic control)

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.sc: You are shown blood results from a patient with suspected acute kidney injury.
tk: Interpret the serum creatinine and urea
Interpret the serum potassium and comment on any risk
Classify the severity using standard AKI criteria
Suggest possible pre-renal, renal, and post-renal causes
State the immediate management priorities
ck: Correctly identifies elevated creatinine/urea consistent with AKI
Correctly identifies hyperkalemia and its cardiac risk
Applies appropriate staging criteria correctly
Lists relevant differentials across pre-renal, renal, post-renal categories
States correct immediate priorities (e.g., ECG for hyperkalemia, fluid assessment, stop nephrotoxins)

internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.t: Procedure Station: Blood Glucose Monitoring and Insulin Injection Technique
internal-medicine/nephrology-and-endocri.sc: Teach a newly diagnosed type 1 diabetic patient how to check blood glucose and administer insulin.
tk: Explain and demonstrate capillary blood glucose testing
Explain insulin storage and preparation
Demonstrate correct subcutaneous injection technique
Explain the importance of injection site rotation
Advise on recognizing and managing hypoglycemia
ck: Correctly demonstrates finger-prick technique and glucometer use
Correctly explains storage (refrigeration of unopened vials) and mixing if needed
Demonstrates correct needle angle, site cleaning, and injection technique
Explains rotation of sites to prevent lipohypertrophy
Provides correct advice on recognizing and treating hypoglycemia (e.g., fast-acting glucose)

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.sc: A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of left-sided weakness and slurred speech that started 1 hour ago.
tk: Take a focused history establishing the exact time of symptom onset
Ask about stroke risk factors
Ask about other neurological symptoms
State your leading diagnosis
Explain the urgency of further management
ck: Establishes precise time of onset/last known well
Asks about hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, prior stroke/TIA
Asks about visual changes, headache, altered consciousness, sensory symptoms
Correctly identifies acute ischemic stroke as leading diagnosis
Correctly emphasizes time-critical nature and need for urgent imaging/thrombolysis assessment

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.sc: Perform a focused cranial nerve examination on a patient with suspected facial nerve palsy.
tk: Assess facial nerve function (motor)
Distinguish between upper and lower motor neuron patterns
Assess corneal reflex and relevant sensory function
Check for other associated cranial nerve involvement
Summarize findings and suggest a diagnosis
ck: Correctly assesses forehead wrinkling, eye closure, and smile symmetry
Correctly distinguishes forehead-sparing (UMN) versus forehead-involving (LMN) pattern
Correctly tests corneal reflex and relevant trigeminal sensory function
Checks hearing and taste as relevant associated findings
Reaches an accurate, well-reasoned diagnosis (e.g., Bell's palsy)

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.sc: You are given synovial fluid analysis results from a patient with an acutely swollen, painful knee.
tk: Interpret the fluid appearance and white cell count
Interpret the presence or absence of crystals
Distinguish between inflammatory, infective, and crystal arthropathy
State the most likely diagnosis
Suggest the immediate management step
ck: Correctly interprets turbidity and cell count in context
Correctly identifies crystal type if present (negatively birefringent needle-shaped for gout)
Correctly reasons through inflammatory versus septic versus crystal-induced categories
Reaches an accurate diagnosis consistent with the findings given
States appropriate immediate management (e.g., antibiotics if septic, NSAIDs/colchicine if gout)

internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.t: Procedure Station: Lumbar Puncture Counseling and Positioning
internal-medicine/neurology-and-rheumato.sc: A patient requires a lumbar puncture for suspected meningitis. Counsel the patient and demonstrate correct positioning.
tk: Explain the indication and procedure to the patient
Obtain informed consent
Demonstrate correct patient positioning
Describe the anatomical landmarks used for needle insertion
Explain potential complications to the patient
ck: Clearly explains why the procedure is needed and what it involves
Obtains appropriate informed consent addressing risks and benefits
Correctly demonstrates lateral decubitus position with flexed spine (or sitting position)
Correctly identifies the iliac crest line (Tuffier's line) corresponding to L3/L4 level
Explains common complications including post-lumbar puncture headache and bleeding/infection risk

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.sc: A 58-year-old man is scheduled for elective open inguinal hernia repair next week. He has been referred to the pre-admission clinic for assessment. Take a focused preoperative history from this patient.
tk: 1. Take a focused history of the presenting surgical problem and its duration.
2. Elicit relevant past medical, surgical, and anaesthetic history including previous complications.
3. Take a full drug history, including anticoagulants, antiplatelets, and allergies.
4. Assess functional capacity and cardiorespiratory fitness for surgery.
5. Explain to the examiner your plan for preoperative optimisation and consent process.
ck: Establishes nature, duration, and complications of the hernia (e.g., irreducibility, pain)
Elicits comorbidities (cardiac, respiratory, diabetes) and prior anaesthetic problems
Documents all medications including anticoagulants/antiplatelets and true allergies
Assesses exercise tolerance/functional capacity appropriately
Outlines sensible optimisation plan and informed consent discussion

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.sc: A 45-year-old woman presents with a swelling in the right groin that increases on standing. Perform a focused examination of the swelling and demonstrate your findings to the examiner.
tk: 1. Inspect the swelling with the patient standing and lying down.
2. Palpate to determine the site, size, consistency, and reducibility of the swelling.
3. Perform the cough impulse test and comment on your finding.
4. Attempt to differentiate an inguinal from a femoral hernia using surface landmarks.
5. Summarise your findings and state your most likely diagnosis to the examiner.
ck: Inspects swelling in both standing and supine positions appropriately
Palpates correctly to assess site, size, consistency, and reducibility
Elicits and correctly interprets cough impulse
Uses pubic tubercle relationship to differentiate inguinal from femoral hernia
Gives a coherent, correctly reasoned summary and diagnosis

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.sc: You are shown a set of preoperative blood results for a 70-year-old man due to undergo elective bowel resection: haemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 180 micromol/L, INR 1.0.
tk: 1. Identify the abnormalities present in this set of results.
2. Suggest the most likely cause of the anaemia given the MCV.
3. Explain the significance of the potassium result before elective surgery.
4. State what further investigations you would request before proceeding.
5. Advise whether surgery should proceed as planned, be delayed, or need modification.
ck: Correctly identifies microcytic anaemia, renal impairment, and hyperkalaemia
Links microcytic anaemia appropriately to likely iron deficiency/occult blood loss
Recognises hyperkalaemia as a significant perioperative cardiac risk
Requests appropriate further work-up (iron studies, ECG, renal review, colonoscopy correlation)
Gives a safe, justified recommendation regarding proceeding with surgery

general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.t: Procedure Station: Surgical Scrubbing and Gowning
general-surgery/surgical-principles-and-.sc: You are about to assist in an elective laparotomy. Demonstrate the correct technique for surgical hand scrubbing and gowning on this mannequin/model station.
tk: 1. Perform the surgical hand scrub using correct technique and sequence.
2. Dry hands using aseptic technique with a sterile towel.
3. Don a sterile gown correctly without contaminating it.
4. Don sterile gloves using the closed-glove technique.
5. Explain to the examiner the principles of maintaining a sterile field throughout.
ck: Scrubs hands and forearms systematically for the correct duration
Dries hands maintaining asepsis, working from fingers to elbow
Dons gown correctly without touching the outer sterile surface
Uses correct closed-glove technique without contamination
Articulates key sterile field principles accurately

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.sc: A 62-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of difficulty swallowing solid food, progressing to difficulty with liquids, and unintentional weight loss. Take a focused history.
tk: 1. Characterise the dysphagia (onset, progression, solids vs liquids).
2. Ask about associated alarm symptoms including weight loss and odynophagia.
3. Elicit relevant risk factors such as smoking, alcohol, and reflux history.
4. Ask about symptoms suggesting aspiration or regurgitation.
5. Summarise the history and state your leading differential diagnosis.
ck: Establishes progressive solid-to-liquid dysphagia pattern accurately
Screens for alarm features (weight loss, odynophagia, anaemia symptoms)
Elicits smoking, alcohol, and chronic reflux as risk factors
Asks about aspiration, cough, and regurgitation appropriately
Reaches a sensible differential prioritising oesophageal malignancy

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.sc: A 34-year-old man presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain for 6 hours. Perform a focused abdominal examination and report your findings.
tk: 1. Inspect the abdomen for distension, scars, and visible peristalsis.
2. Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, guarding, and rigidity.
3. Elicit rebound tenderness and percussion tenderness appropriately.
4. Auscultate for bowel sounds and comment on findings.
5. State your clinical impression and immediate management priorities.
ck: Systematically inspects abdomen noting relevant signs
Correctly elicits and localises tenderness, guarding, or rigidity
Correctly demonstrates rebound/percussion tenderness technique
Auscultates appropriately and interprets bowel sound findings
Gives coherent impression (e.g., peritonitis) with correct initial management plan

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.t: Data Interpretation: Erect Chest and Abdominal X-ray
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.sc: You are shown an erect chest X-ray and supine abdominal X-ray of a 50-year-old woman with sudden severe abdominal pain. The erect chest X-ray shows free air under the right hemidiaphragm.
tk: 1. Identify the abnormal finding on the erect chest X-ray.
2. State the clinical significance of this finding.
3. List three possible underlying causes for this finding.
4. State what additional imaging or investigation may be useful.
5. Outline the immediate management priorities for this patient.
ck: Correctly identifies free subdiaphragmatic air (pneumoperitoneum)
Explains this indicates a perforated hollow viscus requiring urgent action
Lists plausible causes (perforated peptic ulcer, perforated diverticulum, perforated appendix/malignancy)
Suggests appropriate further imaging (CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast)
Outlines correct emergency management (resuscitation, analgesia, antibiotics, urgent surgical referral)

general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.t: Procedure Station: Nasogastric Tube Insertion and Confirmation
general-surgery/gi-surgery-esophagus-sto.sc: A 55-year-old man with a suspected bowel obstruction requires insertion of a nasogastric tube for decompression. Demonstrate the procedure on the manikin.
tk: 1. Explain the procedure to the patient and obtain verbal consent.
2. Measure the correct length of tube to be inserted using surface landmarks.
3. Insert the nasogastric tube using correct technique.
4. Confirm correct tube placement using an appropriate bedside method.
5. Describe how you would secure the tube and document the procedure.
ck: Explains procedure clearly and obtains appropriate consent
Correctly measures nose-ear-xiphisternum distance for tube length
Inserts tube smoothly with correct patient positioning and technique
Confirms placement appropriately (pH aspirate testing, correct interpretation)
Secures tube properly and documents length, confirmation method, and time

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.t: History Taking: Right Upper Quadrant Pain
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.sc: A 40-year-old obese woman presents with recurrent episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Take a focused history from this patient.
tk: 1. Characterise the pain (site, radiation, timing, relation to food).
2. Ask about associated symptoms including nausea, vomiting, fever, and jaundice.
3. Elicit risk factors for gallstone disease.
4. Ask about symptoms suggesting complications such as cholangitis or pancreatitis.
5. Summarise findings and state your leading diagnosis.
ck: Elicits classic biliary colic pattern related to fatty food intake
Screens for fever, jaundice, nausea and vomiting appropriately
Identifies relevant risk factors (female, fertile, forty, fat, family history)
Screens for red-flag features of cholangitis (Charcot's triad) or pancreatitis
Reaches an appropriate diagnosis of biliary colic/cholelithiasis with correct differentials

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.t: Clinical Examination: Jaundice and Hepatobiliary Examination
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.sc: A 65-year-old man presents with painless progressive jaundice and weight loss. Perform a focused examination relevant to his presentation.
tk: 1. Inspect for signs of jaundice, scratch marks, and chronic liver disease.
2. Palpate the abdomen for hepatomegaly and a palpable gallbladder.
3. Perform and interpret Courvoisier's sign.
4. Examine for signs of metastatic spread (e.g., lymphadenopathy, ascites).
5. State your clinical impression and likely diagnosis.
ck: Correctly identifies jaundice, excoriations, and stigmata of chronic liver disease
Systematically palpates liver and gallbladder for enlargement
Correctly demonstrates and interprets Courvoisier's law
Checks for Virchow's node, ascites, and other metastatic signs
Reaches sensible impression (e.g., malignant biliary obstruction, likely pancreatic head cancer)

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.t: Data Interpretation: Liver Function Tests in Obstructive Jaundice
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.sc: You are shown liver function tests of a 60-year-old man with jaundice: total bilirubin 180 micromol/L (mostly conjugated), ALP markedly raised, GGT markedly raised, ALT and AST mildly raised, albumin normal.
tk: 1. Describe the pattern of liver function test abnormality shown.
2. State whether this pattern suggests a hepatocellular or cholestatic process.
3. List three possible causes for this pattern in this age group.
4. State what initial imaging investigation you would request.
5. Outline your next steps in management based on your interpretation.
ck: Correctly identifies a cholestatic/obstructive pattern of LFT derangement
Correctly distinguishes cholestatic from hepatocellular pattern
Suggests plausible causes (choledocholithiasis, pancreatic head mass, cholangiocarcinoma)
Requests appropriate first-line imaging (abdominal ultrasound)
Outlines a logical next-step management/referral pathway (MRCP, ERCP, surgical referral)

general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.t: Procedure Station: Abdominal Drain Care and Removal Technique
general-surgery/hepatobiliary-and-pancre.sc: A patient is 5 days post cholecystectomy with an abdominal drain in situ, now draining minimal serous fluid. Demonstrate assessment and removal of the drain on this model.
tk: 1. Explain the procedure to the patient and confirm indications for removal.
2. Assess the drain site and drainage characteristics before removal.
3. Remove sutures securing the drain using correct technique.
4. Remove the drain smoothly using correct technique and dress the site.
5. Describe what you would document and monitor after removal.
ck: Explains procedure and confirms clinical criteria for safe removal
Appropriately assesses drain output volume, character, and site condition
Removes securing sutures correctly without injury
Removes drain smoothly with correct technique and applies appropriate dressing
States correct post-removal monitoring and documentation requirements

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.sc: A 38-year-old woman presents with a lump in her left breast noticed two weeks ago. Take a focused history relevant to this presentation.
tk: 1. Characterise the lump (onset, change with menstrual cycle, associated pain).
2. Ask about nipple discharge, skin changes, or nipple retraction.
3. Elicit relevant risk factors including family history of breast/ovarian cancer.
4. Ask about menstrual, reproductive, and hormonal history.
5. Summarise the history and outline your next steps in assessment.
ck: Establishes lump characteristics and cyclical relationship appropriately
Screens for nipple discharge and skin/nipple changes
Elicits family history and other relevant breast cancer risk factors
Takes appropriate menstrual/reproductive/hormonal history
Proposes correct triple assessment pathway as next step

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.sc: A 45-year-old woman presents for assessment of a palpable lump in her right breast. Perform a focused clinical breast examination and present your findings.
tk: 1. Inspect both breasts with the patient in appropriate positions.
2. Palpate the breast systematically to characterise the lump.
3. Examine both axillae and supraclavicular regions for lymphadenopathy.
4. Assess for skin tethering, peau d'orange, or nipple involvement.
5. Present a structured summary of findings and likely diagnosis.
ck: Inspects breasts appropriately in sitting/arms-raised positions with consent
Palpates systematically describing site, size, consistency, mobility of lump
Correctly examines axillary and supraclavicular lymph node regions
Assesses for skin/nipple changes suggestive of malignancy
Gives clear, well-organised summary and reasonable differential diagnosis

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.sc: A 30-year-old woman presents with a neck swelling. Thyroid function tests show: TSH markedly suppressed, free T4 elevated, free T3 elevated.
tk: 1. Interpret the thyroid function test pattern shown.
2. State the likely clinical diagnosis based on this pattern.
3. List three possible underlying causes for this biochemical picture.
4. State what further investigation would help confirm the underlying cause.
5. Outline the general treatment options available for this condition.
ck: Correctly identifies a primary hyperthyroid biochemical pattern
Correctly links pattern to clinical hyperthyroidism
Lists plausible causes (Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma)
Suggests appropriate confirmatory test (TSH receptor antibodies, radionuclide uptake scan)
Outlines correct treatment options (antithyroid drugs, radioiodine, surgery)

general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.t: Procedure Station: Breast Lump Marking and Fine Needle Aspiration Counseling
general-surgery/breast-and-endocrine-sur.sc: A patient with a palpable breast lump requires counseling and preparation for fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC). Demonstrate the pre-procedure steps on this model.
tk: 1. Explain the FNAC procedure and its purpose to the patient in simple terms.
2. Obtain informed consent, addressing the patient's concerns.
3. Correctly position the patient and identify/mark the lump for sampling.
4. Describe the correct technique for performing the aspiration.
5. Explain how the sample will be processed and when results will be available.
ck: Explains procedure clearly, appropriately, and reassuringly
Obtains valid informed consent addressing patient concerns
Correctly positions patient and accurately marks/palpates the lesion
Describes correct needle technique and aspiration method
Explains sample handling and realistic timeline for results

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.sc: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with inability to pass urine for 10 hours and severe suprapubic pain. Take a focused history.
tk: 1. Characterise the onset and associated lower urinary tract symptoms.
2. Ask about precipitating factors including medications and constipation.
3. Elicit relevant past history including prostate disease or previous retention.
4. Screen for red flag features suggesting spinal cord compression.
5. Summarise the history and state your immediate management priority.
ck: Establishes acute retention with associated LUTS (hesitancy, poor stream, nocturia)
Identifies precipitating factors (anticholinergics, opioids, alcohol, constipation)
Elicits relevant prostatic history and prior episodes
Screens appropriately for cauda equina/cord compression red flags
Correctly prioritises urgent urethral catheterisation as immediate management

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.sc: A 66-year-old man with diabetes presents with pain in his left calf on walking that resolves with rest. Perform a focused peripheral vascular examination of the lower limbs.
tk: 1. Inspect both lower limbs for colour, hair loss, ulcers, and gangrene.
2. Palpate temperature and capillary refill in both limbs.
3. Palpate all major peripheral pulses in both lower limbs.
4. Perform Buerger's test and interpret the finding.
5. Summarise your findings and state the likely diagnosis.
ck: Inspects for pallor, trophic changes, ulceration, and hair loss appropriately
Assesses temperature gradient and capillary refill correctly
Systematically palpates femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses
Correctly performs and interprets Buerger's test
Reaches correct diagnosis of peripheral arterial disease/intermittent claudication

general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.t: Data Interpretation: Renal Function and Urinalysis
general-surgery/urology-and-vascular-sur.sc: You are shown urinalysis and blood results for a 55-year-old man with loin pain and haematuria: urinalysis shows blood 3+, no protein or nitrites; serum creatinine 95 micromol/L; serum calcium mildly elevated.
tk: 1. Identify the significant findings in the results shown.
2. Suggest the most likely underlying diagnosis given loin pain and haematuria.
3. Explain the possible relevance of the mildly elevated calcium.
4. State what imaging investigation you would request first.
5. Outline the initial management approach for this presentation.
ck: Correctly identifies non-visible/microscopic haematuria without infection features
Suggests renal/ureteric calculus as the leading diagnosis
Appropriately links elevated calcium to possible hyperparathyroidism as a stone risk factor
Requests appropriate first-line imaging (non-contrast CT KUB or renal ultrasound)

ck: Correctly identifies right axis deviation and RVH pattern
Correctly notes some right heart dominance is normal in neonates but interprets in clinical context
Suggests a plausible duct-dependent cyanotic lesion (e.g., Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition)
Correctly suggests pulse oximetry/hyperoxia test as initial assessment
Correctly identifies prostaglandin E1 to maintain ductal patency as an urgent priority

pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.t: Procedure Station: Nebulizer/Inhaler Technique for Childhood Asthma
pediatrics/pediatric-respiratory-and-car.sc: A 6-year-old child newly diagnosed with asthma requires teaching on correct inhaler technique using a spacer device. Demonstrate this counseling station.
tk: 1. Explain the purpose of the spacer device for this age group.
2. Demonstrate correct assembly and priming of the inhaler and spacer.
3. Demonstrate correct technique for administering a dose via the spacer.
4. Explain how to recognise correct versus incorrect technique.
5. Advise on cleaning of the device and when to seek medical review.
ck: Explains rationale for spacer use in young children clearly
Correctly demonstrates assembly and shaking/priming of inhaler
Correctly demonstrates single-breath or tidal-breathing technique via spacer
Correctly identifies signs of poor technique (e.g., mask/mouthpiece seal)
Gives correct device cleaning advice and appropriate safety-netting

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.t: History Taking: Acute Diarrhoea and Dehydration
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.sc: A mother brings her 1-year-old child with 3 days of watery diarrhoea and vomiting. Take a focused history to assess hydration status and cause.
tk: 1. Characterise the diarrhoea and vomiting including frequency and content.
2. Ask about urine output and signs of dehydration noticed by the parent.
3. Ask about oral intake and tolerance of fluids at home.
4. Screen for red flag symptoms including blood in stool or lethargy.
5. Summarise the history and give your assessment of hydration status.
ck: Characterises stool/vomiting frequency, volume, and content appropriately
Assesses urine output and parent-reported dehydration signs
Establishes oral intake and fluid tolerance at home
Screens for red flags (blood in stool, reduced consciousness, bilious vomiting)
Gives a sensible clinical assessment of dehydration severity

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.t: Clinical Examination: Assessment of Dehydration in a Child
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.sc: A 2-year-old child presents with diarrhoea and reduced oral intake. Perform a focused clinical examination to assess the degree of dehydration.
tk: 1. Assess the child's general appearance, alertness, and activity.
2. Assess skin turgor and mucous membrane moisture.
3. Assess capillary refill time and peripheral perfusion.
4. Check for a sunken fontanelle and sunken eyes if applicable.
5. Summarise your findings and classify the degree of dehydration.
ck: Correctly assesses general appearance and alertness
Correctly assesses skin turgor and mucous membranes
Correctly measures and interprets capillary refill time
Correctly checks fontanelle and eyes for signs of dehydration
Gives correct classification of dehydration severity (no/some/severe dehydration)

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.t: Data Interpretation: Urinalysis in Suspected Nephrotic Syndrome
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.sc: You are shown investigation results of a 4-year-old child with facial swelling: urinalysis shows protein 4+, no blood; serum albumin low; serum cholesterol elevated.
tk: 1. Identify the significant abnormalities shown in these results.
2. State the clinical syndrome that this combination of findings suggests.
3. Explain the pathophysiological link between proteinuria and the low albumin.
4. State what other clinical feature would support this diagnosis.
5. Outline the general management approach for this condition.
ck: Correctly identifies heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and hyperlipidaemia
Correctly diagnoses nephrotic syndrome based on this triad
Correctly explains urinary protein loss causing hypoalbuminaemia
Correctly identifies oedema (e.g., periorbital/facial) as a supporting feature
Outlines appropriate management (corticosteroids as first-line, salt/fluid management)

pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.t: Procedure Station: Oral Rehydration Therapy Counseling
pediatrics/pediatric-gi-renal-and-geneti.sc: A mother brings her 18-month-old child with mild dehydration from gastroenteritis. Demonstrate counseling on oral rehydration therapy for this station.
tk: 1. Explain the purpose and composition of oral rehydration solution.
2. Demonstrate/explain correct preparation of the oral rehydration solution.
3. Explain the recommended volume and frequency of administration.
4. Advise on continued feeding and breastfeeding during the illness.
5. Explain warning signs that should prompt the parent to seek urgent medical review.
ck: Explains purpose and appropriate composition of ORS clearly
Correctly explains preparation technique and dilution
Gives correct guidance on volume/frequency of administration
Correctly advises on continuing feeds/breastfeeding during illness
Gives accurate and complete safety-netting/warning signs advice

ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-ante.sc: A 30-year-old man presents with a painful red right eye for one day. Take a focused history relevant to this presentation.
tk: 1. Characterise the pain, redness, and any associated discharge.
2. Ask about visual changes including blurring or photophobia.
3. Ask about contact lens use and any history of trauma.
4. Screen for red flag symptoms suggesting a sight-threatening cause.
5. Summarise the history and state your leading and urgent differential diagnoses.
ck: Characterises pain, redness, and discharge appropriately
Screens for visual acuity change and photophobia
Elicits contact lens use and trauma history
Screens correctly for red flags (severe pain, marked photophobia, visual loss)
Reaches sensible differential including sight-threatening causes to exclude

ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-ante.t: Clinical Examination: External Eye and Anterior Segment Examination
ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-ante.sc: A 45-year-old woman presents with a red, irritated left eye. Perform a focused external and anterior segment examination.
tk: 1. Assess visual acuity in both eyes before proceeding.
2. Inspect the eyelids, conjunctiva, and sclera for abnormality.
3. Examine the cornea for clarity and any visible defect.
4. Assess pupil size, shape, and reaction to light.
5. Summarise your findings and state your likely diagnosis.
ck: Correctly assesses and documents visual acuity in both eyes
Systematically inspects eyelids, conjunctiva, and sclera
Correctly examines cornea for clarity/defects
Correctly assesses pupil size, shape, and light reaction
Gives coherent summary and sensible working diagnosis

ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-ante.t: Data Interpretation: Intraocular Pressure and Visual Field Findings
ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-ante.sc: You are shown results for a 60-year-old man: intraocular pressure right eye 32 mmHg, left eye 30 mmHg, with visual field testing showing peripheral field loss bilaterally and cup-to-disc ratio of 0.8.
tk: 1. Interpret the intraocular pressure values shown.
2. Interpret the visual field and cup-to-disc ratio findings.
3. State the most likely diagnosis based on this combination of findings.
4. Explain why peripheral vision is typically affected before central vision in this condition.
5. Outline the general treatment options available for this condition.
ck: Correctly identifies elevated intraocular pressure bilaterally
Correctly interprets peripheral field loss and increased cup-to-disc ratio as glaucomatous
Correctly diagnoses primary open-angle glaucoma
Explains peripheral-before-central visual loss pattern in glaucoma correctly
Outlines correct treatment options (topical medications, laser, surgery)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-ante.t: Procedure Station: Eye Irrigation for Chemical Injury
ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-ante.sc: A patient presents immediately after an alkali splash to the right eye. Demonstrate the immediate management of ocular irrigation on this model.
tk: 1. State the priority of immediate irrigation before any other assessment.
2. Demonstrate correct positioning of the patient for irrigation.
3. Demonstrate correct technique for continuous eye irrigation including eyelid eversion.
4. State how you would confirm irrigation has been adequate.
5. Describe what assessment and referral is needed after irrigation.
ck: Correctly prioritises immediate irrigation over history/examination
Positions patient correctly (head tilted, affected side down)
Demonstrates correct continuous irrigation technique including eyelid eversion to remove particulate matter
Correctly states use of pH testing to confirm adequate irrigation
Describes correct need for visual acuity assessment and urgent ophthalmology referral

ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-post.t: History Taking: Sudden Painless Visual Loss
ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-post.sc: A 68-year-old man presents with sudden painless loss of vision in his right eye. Take a focused history relevant to this presentation.
tk: 1. Characterise the onset and pattern of visual loss.
2. Ask about associated symptoms such as floaters, flashes, or a curtain-like field defect.
3. Ask about vascular risk factors and relevant past medical history.
4. Screen for symptoms suggestive of giant cell arteritis.
5. Summarise the history and state your leading differential diagnoses.
ck: Establishes sudden, painless onset and pattern of visual loss
Screens for floaters, flashes, and curtain-like field loss
Elicits vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation)
Screens for temporal headache, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness
Reaches sensible differential (retinal detachment, vascular occlusion, GCA) with correct urgency

ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-post.sc: A 55-year-old diabetic patient presents for a routine eye check. Demonstrate correct technique for direct ophthalmoscopy on this model/patient.
tk: 1. Explain the procedure to the patient and dim the room lights appropriately.
2. Set up the ophthalmoscope correctly and select the appropriate eye/hand.
3. Demonstrate correct approach and technique to visualise the fundus.
4. Systematically examine the optic disc, vessels, macula, and periphery.
5. Describe what diabetic retinopathy changes you would look for.
ck: Explains procedure and dims room appropriately
Correctly sets up ophthalmoscope and uses correct eye/hand for the patient's eye examined
Demonstrates correct approach angle and technique to obtain a red reflex and view fundus
Systematically examines disc, vessels, macula, and periphery
Correctly describes relevant diabetic retinopathy signs (microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, neovascularisation)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-post.t: Data Interpretation: Visual Acuity and Refraction Chart
ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-post.sc: You are shown visual acuity results for a 10-year-old child: unaided vision right eye 6/6, left eye 6/24, improving to 6/6 with pinhole in the left eye.
tk: 1. Interpret the visual acuity results shown for each eye.
2. Explain the significance of improvement with a pinhole in the left eye.
3. State the most likely cause of the reduced vision in the left eye.
4. Explain the risk of amblyopia if this is left uncorrected in a child this age.
5. Outline the appropriate management for this child.
ck: Correctly interprets unilateral reduced vision in the left eye
Correctly explains pinhole improvement indicates a refractive cause
Correctly identifies uncorrected refractive error as the likely cause
Correctly explains risk of amblyopia developing with delayed correction in childhood
Outlines correct management (refractive correction, possible patching, ophthalmology referral)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-post.t: Procedure Station: Visual Acuity Testing with Snellen Chart
ophthalmology-and-ent/ophthalmology-post.sc: A patient presents for a routine vision assessment. Demonstrate correct technique for testing visual acuity using a Snellen chart.
tk: 1. Position the patient at the correct testing distance from the chart.
2. Test each eye separately, occluding the other eye appropriately.
3. Record the smallest line the patient can read correctly for each eye.
4. Demonstrate use of a pinhole if visual acuity is reduced.
5. Correctly document the visual acuity results using standard notation.
ck: Positions patient at correct standard testing distance
Tests each eye separately with correct occlusion technique
Correctly identifies and records smallest readable line per eye
Correctly demonstrates pinhole use when acuity is reduced
Documents results using correct standard notation (e.g., 6/6, 6/12)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A 65-year-old man presents with gradually progressive hearing loss in both ears. Take a focused history relevant to this presentation.
tk: 1. Characterise the onset, progression, and laterality of the hearing loss.
2. Ask about associated symptoms including tinnitus and vertigo.
3. Ask about relevant risk factors including noise exposure and ototoxic medication use.
4. Screen for symptoms suggesting a conductive versus sensorineural cause.
5. Summarise the history and state your leading diagnosis.
ck: Establishes gradual, bilateral, progressive pattern of hearing loss
Screens for tinnitus and vertigo appropriately
Elicits noise exposure history and ototoxic drug use
Distinguishes features suggestive of conductive vs sensorineural loss
Reaches sensible diagnosis (e.g., presbycusis) with appropriate reasoning

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A 6-year-old child presents with ear pain and fever. Perform a focused otoscopic examination on this model/patient.
tk: 1. Explain the procedure to the child/parent in an age-appropriate manner.
2. Correctly select and hold the otoscope for examination.
3. Correctly straighten the ear canal appropriate to the patient's age.
4. Systematically examine the ear canal and tympanic membrane.
5. Describe the expected otoscopic findings in acute otitis media.
ck: Explains procedure appropriately for age and reassures patient/parent
Correctly holds otoscope with appropriate hand support/stabilisation
Correctly pulls pinna to straighten canal appropriate to patient age (up/back for adults, down/back for young children)
Systematically inspects canal and tympanic membrane
Correctly describes findings of acute otitis media (bulging, erythematous, opaque membrane)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: You are shown a pure tone audiogram showing air conduction thresholds elevated with air-bone gap present, bone conduction thresholds within normal limits, in the right ear.
tk: 1. Describe the pattern shown on this audiogram.
2. State whether this represents a conductive, sensorineural, or mixed hearing loss.
3. List three possible causes for this type of hearing loss.
4. State what examination finding you would look for to support the diagnosis.
5. Outline the possible management options for this type of hearing loss.
ck: Correctly describes air-bone gap with normal bone conduction
Correctly classifies this as a conductive hearing loss
Lists plausible causes (otitis media with effusion, otosclerosis, wax impaction)
Suggests correct examination correlation (otoscopy for effusion/wax)
Outlines correct management options (medical treatment, grommets, hearing aid, stapedectomy as appropriate)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.t: Procedure Station: Ear Syringing/Irrigation for Wax Removal
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A patient presents with conductive hearing loss due to impacted ear wax confirmed on otoscopy. Demonstrate the procedure for ear irrigation on this model.
tk: 1. Confirm there are no contraindications to irrigation before proceeding.
2. Explain the procedure to the patient and obtain consent.
3. Position the patient and equipment correctly for safe irrigation.
4. Demonstrate correct technique for irrigating the ear canal.
5. Re-examine the ear canal after the procedure and advise the patient appropriately.
ck: Correctly checks for contraindications (perforation, prior ear surgery, infection)
Explains procedure clearly and obtains consent
Positions patient and irrigation equipment correctly and safely
Demonstrates correct irrigation technique directing flow along the canal wall
Re-examines canal post-procedure and gives appropriate aftercare advice

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A 35-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of nasal blockage and reduced sense of smell. Take a focused history relevant to this presentation.
tk: 1. Characterise the nasal obstruction (unilateral/bilateral, constant/intermittent).
2. Ask about associated symptoms including discharge, facial pain, and anosmia.
3. Ask about history of allergy, asthma, or aspirin sensitivity.
4. Screen for red flag symptoms suggesting malignancy.
5. Summarise the history and state your leading differential diagnosis.
ck: Characterises laterality and pattern of nasal obstruction
Screens for discharge, facial pain, and anosmia appropriately
Elicits atopic history and aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease features
Screens for red flags (unilateral bleeding, epistaxis, facial numbness)
Reaches sensible differential (e.g., nasal polyposis, allergic rhinitis) with correct reasoning

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A patient presents with nasal obstruction and clear rhinorrhoea. Perform a focused anterior rhinoscopy examination.
tk: 1. Explain the procedure to the patient and position them correctly.
2. Use the nasal speculum and headlight/light source correctly.
3. Systematically inspect the nasal septum, turbinates, and nasal mucosa.
4. Look specifically for nasal polyps or other masses.
5. Summarise your findings and state your likely diagnosis.
ck: Explains procedure and positions patient appropriately
Correctly uses nasal speculum and adequate light source
Systematically inspects septum, turbinates, and mucosal appearance
Specifically screens for and correctly identifies polyps/masses if present
Gives coherent summary and sensible diagnosis

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.t: Data Interpretation: Sinus CT Scan Findings
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: You are shown a CT scan report of the paranasal sinuses of a patient with chronic facial pain: bilateral mucosal thickening in the maxillary sinuses with opacification, and osteomeatal complex obstruction noted.
tk: 1. Identify the key abnormal findings described in this report.

ck: Correctly identifies bilateral mucosal thickening and sinus opacification
Correctly diagnoses chronic rhinosinusitis
Correctly explains role of osteomeatal complex obstruction in impairing sinus drainage
Correctly outlines first-line conservative management (nasal saline, intranasal steroids, antibiotics if indicated)
Correctly identifies functional endoscopic sinus surgery as the surgical option

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.t: Procedure Station: Management of Acute Epistaxis
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with active bleeding from the right nostril. Demonstrate the initial management of epistaxis on this model.
tk: 1. Assess the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation before local measures.
2. Demonstrate correct first aid technique for nasal pressure application.
3. Position the patient correctly during first aid measures.
4. Describe how you would identify the bleeding point if bleeding persists.
5. Outline the next steps in management if first aid measures fail to control bleeding.
ck: Correctly performs initial ABC assessment before local treatment
Demonstrates correct technique (firm pressure on the cartilaginous nasal septum)
Correctly positions patient (sitting forward, head tilted slightly down)
Describes correct use of nasal speculum/light source to identify bleeding point (e.g., Little's area)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A 55-year-old man, heavy smoker, presents with hoarseness of voice for 8 weeks. Take a focused history relevant to this presentation.
tk: 1. Characterise the onset and duration of the voice change.
2. Ask about associated symptoms including dysphagia and weight loss.
3. Elicit relevant risk factors including smoking and alcohol use.
4. Screen for symptoms suggesting airway compromise.
5. Summarise the history and state your priority diagnosis to exclude.
ck: Establishes duration and persistence of hoarseness (>3 weeks is significant)
Screens for dysphagia, weight loss, and haemoptysis
Elicits smoking and alcohol history as risk factors
Screens for stridor or breathing difficulty suggesting airway compromise
Correctly prioritises laryngeal malignancy as the diagnosis to exclude

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A 40-year-old woman presents with a swelling in the anterior neck. Perform a focused examination of the neck lump.
tk: 1. Inspect the neck for the swelling and ask the patient to swallow.
2. Palpate the lump to assess site, size, consistency, and mobility.
3. Ask the patient to protrude the tongue and observe the swelling's movement.
4. Examine for associated cervical lymphadenopathy.
5. Summarise your findings and state your likely diagnosis.
ck: Correctly inspects and observes movement of swelling on swallowing
Correctly palpates lump characteristics systematically
Correctly tests for movement with tongue protrusion (thyroglossal cyst)
Systematically examines cervical lymph node regions
Gives coherent summary and sensible differential (e.g., thyroid swelling)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.t: Data Interpretation: Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology of Neck Mass
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: You are shown an FNAC report of a 45-year-old woman with a thyroid nodule: cytology shows follicular cells with nuclear grooves and intranuclear inclusions, reported as suspicious for papillary carcinoma.
tk: 1. Interpret the cytological findings described in this report.

3. Explain why FNAC is the first-line investigation for a thyroid nodule.

ck: Correctly interprets nuclear grooves/inclusions as suspicious features
Correctly identifies papillary thyroid carcinoma as the likely diagnosis
Correctly explains FNAC's role as a minimally invasive first-line test
Suggests appropriate further work-up (thyroid function tests, neck ultrasound, staging)
Outlines correct management (surgery, possible radioiodine, thyroid hormone suppression)

ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.t: Procedure Station: Peritonsillar Abscess Assessment and Airway Safety
ophthalmology-and-ent/ent-diseases-of-th.sc: A 20-year-old man presents with severe sore throat, trismus, and a muffled voice. Demonstrate the focused assessment of this suspected peritonsillar abscess on the model.
tk: 1. Assess the airway as a priority given the presentation.
2. Inspect the oral cavity and oropharynx as far as trismus allows.
3. Describe the expected clinical signs of a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy).
4. State the initial emergency management priorities for this patient.
5. Describe the definitive procedure used to treat this condition.
ck: Correctly prioritises airway assessment given trismus/muffled voice
Attempts safe oropharyngeal inspection within limits of trismus
Correctly describes expected signs (uvular deviation, unilateral swelling, trismus)
Correctly outlines emergency priorities (IV fluids, analgesia, antibiotics, ENT referral)
Correctly describes needle aspiration or incision and drainage as definitive treatment
